# Agent Contract

For architecture choices, component design, bounded evidence investigation,
testing, or maintenance, consult [agent_building.md](agent_building.md).
That optional engineering reference complements the required runtime interfaces
below; it does not add required architectures or evaluation criteria.

## How the agent is run

Each evaluation case is a conversation with one developer. After each
developer message the agent may call tools, one or more rounds, and then
answers with text; that text is its reply to the developer. The developer ends
the conversation.

The developer writes what they came to say, one message per agent reply,
whatever that reply was. They do not answer questions asked in chat text. To
learn a fact they have not written, the agent calls `ask_developer` with the
fields it needs; each answer is the developer's own words, or that they don't
have it:

| Field | What the developer tells you |
|---|---|
| `org_id` | Their org or account id |
| `invoice_id`, `invoice_month` | The invoice, or the billing month, they mean |
| `line_items`, `amounts` | The invoice lines and the amounts they see or expected |
| `request_ids`, `response_status` | Request ids they have, and the HTTP status those requests returned |
| `time_of_issue`, `timezone` | When it happened (and how long ago), and the timezone they used |
| `checks_done` | What they already checked or know about how they call the API: filters, how they counted, client retries or timeouts |
| `plan`, `contract` | Their plan, and whether they have a contract and what it covers |
| `error_code` | The error or decline code they saw |
| `billing_period` | The usage period they mean | To get the developer's
approval for an action, the agent calls `confirm_with_developer` with exactly
what it will do; the answer is `yes` or `no`, with the developer's words. Both
tools come from `redwood_kit.developer.DeveloperTools`, already mixed into the
starter `Tools`.

At the end of your session the evaluator copies `workspace/` to a read-only
directory and runs the agent from there, as an unprivileged user without API
credentials. The working directory is the frozen workspace, and it is the only
part of the filesystem the agent can read: `/app/R` and everything else
outside the workspace are not available at runtime. `redwood_kit`, the Python
standard library, `pydantic`, and `openai` are importable.

## What you deliver

The support agent is the workspace. `agent.py` and `tools.py` are required
entry points. Deliver at least one functional skill and one functional subagent
for the billing-support job. Choose their responsibilities, prompts, tools,
and integration. The example files are format stubs; replace them or remove
them and create real components. Also deliver at least one functional `@hook`
guardrail for this job. The remaining files provide the conventions below.

| Workspace file | Purpose |
|----------------|---------|
| `system_prompt.md` | Identity: who the agent is, whose interests it serves, and its authority. Not the billing rulebook. |
| `AGENTS.md` | Operating principles: how the agent retrieves, checks evidence, and hands off. Exact billing rules do not go here. A developer can't override them. |
| `tools.py` | The actions the agent can take (`@is_tool` methods on `Tools`). `load_skill`, `delegate`, `ask_developer` and `confirm_with_developer` are already mixed in. |
| `hooks.py` | Guardrails the runtime runs around every developer message and tool call (`@hook` methods on `Hooks`). At least one functional guardrail is required. |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | A procedure the model loads when needed. At least one substantive billing-support procedure is required. |
| `subagents/<name>.md` | A specialist with its own prompt, model, and tools in a separate context. At least one functional billing-support specialist is required. |
| `agent.py` | The agent itself: loads the files above and runs the model. Entry point for the evaluator. It already lists the skills and subagents it finds. |

You may add any other files or modules under `workspace/`.

## The factory function

`workspace/agent.py` must export `create_agent()`:

```python
from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context

def create_agent():
    context = get_agent_context()
    ...  # return an object with get_init_state() and generate_next_message()
```

`get_agent_context()` is available while the factory runs and returns:

- `action_interface`: `.available` is the tuple of every `@is_tool` action from
  `workspace/tools.py` (each has `.name`, `.description`, `.parameters`);
  `.select([...names])` picks a subset.
- `resources`: `.root` (the frozen workspace), `.files` (relative inventory),
  `.path(relative)` and `.read_text(relative)`.
- `model_gateway`: the only inference path. `.models` lists the allowed
  `ModelConfig`s; `.generate(model=..., messages=[...], actions=None,
  tool_choice=None, **inference_args)` returns an `AssistantMessage` whose
  `.content` or `.tool_calls` is set (`.usage` carries token counts).
  `tool_choice` takes `"auto"` (default), `"none"`, `"required"` or
  `{"type": "function", "name": ...}`; whether the deployed model honours a
  forced call is up to that model.
  `.embed(model=..., inputs=[...], **kwargs)` returns one vector per input, in
  order. `.embedding_models` lists the allowed embedding models. Calls must
  satisfy `framework/deployment_manifest.json`: a fixed value is applied for
  you (passing a different one is an error), and a constraint of the form
  `{"one_of": [...]}` is a choice you pass on every call. Embedding calls
  take no extra arguments.
- `runtime_config`: `{"company": "Redwood Inference", "role": "billing_support"}`.
- `billing`: Redwood's billing console (see "Billing console"), also
  available to tools as `self.billing`.

Anything workspace code prints goes to the agent's log, not to the developer.

## The turn interface

- `get_init_state(message_history=None) -> state` — called once per case with
  the agent's fixed greeting, `"Hi! How can I help you today?"`, as the first
  message of `message_history`.
- `generate_next_message(message, state) -> (AssistantMessage, state)` — called
  with each developer `UserMessage`, and with a `ToolMessage` (or a
  `MultiToolMessage`, `.tool_messages`) after each round of tool calls. Tool
  results are JSON text in `.content`; a failed call has `.error == True`.

An `AssistantMessage` carries text for the developer or tool calls, never both.
`ModelGateway.generate` drops narration that accompanies tool calls, so a
message returned straight from the gateway is always valid.

## Tools

`workspace/tools.py` defines `class Tools(ToolKitBase)`. Every method decorated
with `@is_tool(...)` is an action: its name is the method name, its description
the docstring summary, and its parameters come from the type hints and the
docstring's `Args:` section. A tool that raises returns a failed tool result to
the agent instead of ending the case.

```python
from redwood_kit.toolkit import ToolKitBase, ToolType, is_tool

class Tools(ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.READ)
    def example(self, query: str) -> dict:
        """One-line description the model sees.

        Args:
            query: What the model should pass.
        """
        ...
```

## Retrieval and file fetch

Choose the knowledge representation and retrieval workflow. The kit does not
chunk or search for you. The index is a LanceDB table: vector search, text
search, or both. The support agent answers from the chunks that search
returns. Do not store full source records for a later read. Exact billing
rules stay in those retrieved chunks. Ship all runtime knowledge in the
read-only workspace; the support agent cannot access `/app/R`.

LanceDB is installed. Put gateway vectors and the source text in one table,
then build a full-text index on that text. Search with a vector, with text,
or with both:

```python
table.search(query_type="hybrid").vector(query_vector).text(query_text).limit(8).to_list()
```

Compute the stored vectors and `query_vector` with `redwood_kit.embeddings.embed`
at build time and `self.gateway.embed` at runtime. Both run the same local
model (`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, 384 dimensions, CPU; no API key).
It reads at most 256 tokens (about 1,000 characters) per text and ignores the
rest, and embeds roughly 28 such texts per second on this container. Pass the
texts in one call; it batches internally. Do not use LanceDB's own embedding
functions. Use the model in the deployment manifest for document and query
vectors. NumPy is installed.

Practice questions (`framework/retrieval_probes.json`) and how to read your
retrieval's results on them are described in `framework/offline-rag/README.md`.
There is no scoring service: you judge the retrieved passages yourself.

## Resource limits

The builder has 7200 seconds in R0 and 3600 seconds in R1, in a container with
2 CPUs, 8 GiB memory, and 20 GiB storage. Besides your own model provider, it
has no network access; embeddings run locally. The deployed support model is
set for each run by the `SUPPORT_MODEL` parameter (a LiteLLM model id);
`framework/deployment_manifest.json` names it exactly, and
it is the only model the agent may call. It is
reachable only through practice conversations (see Practice conversations). The support process has a 4 GiB address-space limit, a
128 MiB per-file write limit, and no direct external network access. Runtime
libraries include LanceDB and `numpy`; nothing can be installed after freezing.

The runtime clock is the conversation's date and time (UTC): `datetime.now()` and `date.today()` in the support process read the moment the developer is writing, not the host's, in graded and practice conversations alike.

A support conversation allows 40 agent turns, including tool rounds. Each
wait for output from the candidate process has a 180-second timeout; gateway
requests have separate provider timeouts and retries. Skills and subagents
share the allowed models. Model inference goes through the runtime gateway.
The complete verifier step has a 3600-second timeout.

## Hooks

`workspace/hooks.py` defines `class Hooks(HookKitBase)`. The runtime runs every
`@hook` method on its event, for every tool call, including those a subagent
makes; hooks for one event run in method-name order. A hook that raises
`Blocked` refuses the call and the model gets the reason; any other exception
is a failed tool result.

```python
from redwood_kit.hooks import Blocked, HookKitBase, hook

class Hooks(HookKitBase):
    @hook("user_message")
    def redact(self, text: str) -> str | None: ...        # replacement text, or None to keep it

    @hook("pre_tool", match="escalate*")
    def check(self, tool: str, args: dict) -> dict | None: ...  # replacement args; raise Blocked to refuse

    @hook("post_tool")
    def trim(self, tool: str, args: dict, result): ...     # replacement result, or None to keep it
```

## Billing console

The runtime provides one billing console as `self.billing` in `Tools` and
`billing` in the build context:

- `describe() -> dict` returns the current tables, field types, references,
  enums, required fields, defaults, and writable flags.
- `query(table, where=None, cursor=None) -> dict` returns `rows` and
  `next_cursor`. Rows are sorted by record key and returned in pages of 25.
  A query requires a scalar value for at least one selector listed by
  `describe()`; other filters may refine the results. Scalar values match list
  fields by containment; list values match by equality.
- `insert(table, row) -> dict` inserts a record and returns its stored row.
- `update(table, row_id, changes) -> dict` updates a record and returns its
  stored row.

`framework/client_api/schema.json` is the current deployment's console
contract and is the same schema returned by `describe()`.
`framework/client_api/practice_cases.json` lists synthetic development cases.
`redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` returns a fresh console over
those records for the current release. It is served by the deployment, like the
graded console; writes last only for that console and nothing is graded.

### Practice conversations

`python -m redwood_kit.practice SCRIPTS.json [--case ID] [--workspace DIR] [--out DIR]`
plays whole conversations with your agent through `redwood_kit.conversation`,
the loop graded conversations use: same greeting, wire protocol, tool rounds,
40-turn limit and resource limits, from a frozen read-only copy of the
workspace. The agent's model calls go to the deployed support model through
the practice model service, embeddings run locally as at grading, billing calls
go to a fresh practice console, and the developer is played from the script.
The developer's opening and agenda lines are worded by the same model and rules
graded conversations use (`redwood_kit.customer`); the developer answers
questions only through `ask_developer`, gives the script's consent answer, and
ends with a transfer after a handoff or a stop when its agenda is used up.

A script is `{"cases": [{"id", "persona", "customer": {"opening", "agenda",
"facts", "confirm", "confirm_reply"}}]}`; `facts` keys are the `ask_developer`
fields. `framework/client_api/practice_conversations.json` has examples over the
practice cases. Each run prints the conversation and writes its transcript,
console calls and developer calls to `--out` (default `/tmp/redwood-practice`).

You have 5 practice conversations per release, each with up to 60 support-model
calls and 40 developer wordings; the service serves nothing else. Choose the
scripts that cover the paths you most need to see working. If it fails or the budget is used
up, the runner stops with an error that says nothing about your agent.

`describe()` is the schema reference for the current console. Credit notes are
insert-only; disputes and cases can be updated while draft and become final
when submitted or escalated. An escalated case hands the case and conversation
so far to its team and finalizes the conversation: every later billing call is
rejected. Writes are final: there is no delete or undo.
The console also rejects a write that breaks one of these rules: a credit
note's or dispute's invoice and lines belong to its account and to each other;
a credit note's amount is positive and at most the lines' uncredited balance;
a dispute's `request_ids` are usage records of the same account; a submitted
dispute needs `invoice_id`, `line_ids`, `reason` and `request_ids`; and an
escalated case needs a `team` and a non-empty `summary`.
The console's schema can change between releases; the runtime `describe()` is authoritative.

A rejected request raises `BillingError` (from `redwood_kit.billing`). Its
message starts with a stable code, also available as `.code`:
`invalid_request` (malformed request or value), `unknown_field`,
`missing_fields`, `not_found` (table, row, or request id), `read_only`,
`not_draft`, `closed` (the conversation was handed off), or `business_rule`
(a valid request that breaks a billing rule, such as crediting more than a
line's balance). Match on the code, not the rest of the message.

Queries and `describe()` are safe to repeat. Inserts and updates are not
idempotent: never retry a write automatically after an error or timeout, or
a credit note may be issued twice. Query the account first to see whether the
write happened. A successful write is visible to the next query in the same
conversation.

## Skills and subagents

Both are required capabilities of the delivered agent. Give the skill a clear
applicability description and actionable procedure. Give the subagent a defined
responsibility, sufficient task context, suitable tools, and a result the
parent agent can use. Wire both into the running agent; files that are merely
present, unchanged stubs, and unreachable code are insufficient. Test loading
the skill and delegating representative work to the subagent. Use them when
appropriate rather than forcing a call in every conversation.

A skill is `workspace/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; a subagent is
`workspace/subagents/<name>.md`. Both start with `---`-fenced `key: value`
lines (no nesting) followed by the body:

- Skill keys: `name`, `description`. The body is the procedure.
- Subagent keys: `name`, `description`, `model` (default: the first allowed
  model), `tools` (comma-separated names
  from `tools.py`, default none), `max_turns` (default 8). The body is its
  system prompt. It sees only that prompt and the task it is given, and returns
  only its final text.

Mix `SkillTools` (a `load_skill` tool) or `SubagentTools` (a `delegate` tool)
from `redwood_kit.skills` and `redwood_kit.subagents` into `Tools` to let the
model use them; `load_skills(path)` and `load_subagents(path)` list them for
your prompt. `run_subagent(spec, task, gateway, runner)` runs one from your own
code.

## Ending a conversation

The runtime also recognizes one optional method on the agent object:

- `is_stop(message) -> bool` — whether an assistant message ends the
  conversation; it ends after that message's tool calls run. Default: the
  agent never signals stop; conversations end from the developer's side or at
  the turn limit.

    @hook("post_tool")
    def trim(self, tool: str, args: dict, result): ...     # replacement result, or None to keep it
```

## Billing console

The runtime provides one billing console as `self.billing` in `Tools` and
`billing` in the build context:

- `describe() -> dict` returns the current tables, field types, references,
  enums, required fields, defaults, and writable flags.
- `query(table, where=None, cursor=None) -> dict` returns `rows` and
  `next_cursor`. Rows are sorted by record key and returned in pages of 25.
  A query requires a scalar value for at least one selector listed by
  `describe()`; other filters may refine the results. Scalar values match list
  fields by containment; list values match by equality.
- `insert(table, row) -> dict` inserts a record and returns its stored row.
- `update(table, row_id, changes) -> dict` updates a record and returns its
  stored row.

`framework/client_api/schema.json` is the current deployment's console
contract and is the same schema returned by `describe()`.
`framework/client_api/practice_cases.json` lists synthetic development cases.
`redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` returns a fresh console over
those records for the current release. It is served by the deployment, like the
graded console; writes last only for that console and nothing is graded.

### Practice conversations

`python -m redwood_kit.practice SCRIPTS.json [--case ID] [--workspace DIR] [--out DIR]`
plays whole conversations with your agent through `redwood_kit.conversation`,
the loop graded conversations use: same greeting, wire protocol, tool rounds,
40-turn limit and resource limits, from a frozen read-only copy of the
workspace. The agent's model calls go to the deployed support model through
the practice model service, embeddings run locally as at grading, billing calls
go to a fresh practice console, and the developer is played from the script.
The developer's opening and agenda lines are worded by the same model and rules
graded conversations use (`redwood_kit.customer`); the developer answers
questions only through `ask_developer`, gives the script's consent answer, and
ends with a transfer after a handoff or a stop when its agenda is used up.

A script is `{"cases": [{"id", "persona", "customer": {"opening", "agenda",
"facts", "confirm", "confirm_reply"}}]}`; `facts` keys are the `ask_developer`
fields. `framework/client_api/practice_conversations.json` has examples over the
practice cases. Each run prints the conversation and writes its transcript,
console calls and developer calls to `--out` (default `/tmp/redwood-practice`).

You have 5 practice conversations per release, each with up to 60 support-model
calls and 40 developer wordings; the service serves nothing else. Choose the
scripts that cover the paths you most need to see working. If it fails or the budget is used
up, the runner stops with an error that says nothing about your agent.

`describe()` is the schema reference for the current console. Credit notes are
insert-only; disputes and cases can be updated while draft and become final
when submitted or escalated. An escalated case hands the case and conversation
so far to its team and finalizes the conversation: every later billing call is
rejected. Writes are final: there is no delete or undo.
The console also rejects a write that breaks one of these rules: a credit
note's or dispute's invoice and lines belong to its account and to each other;
a credit note's amount is positive and at most the lines' uncredited balance;
a dispute's `request_ids` are usage records of the same account; a submitted
dispute needs `invoice_id`, `line_ids`, `reason` and `request_ids`; and an
escalated case needs a `team` and a non-empty `summary`.
The console's schema can change between releases; the runtime `describe()` is authoritative.

A rejected request raises `BillingError` (from `redwood_kit.billing`). Its
message starts with a stable code, also available as `.code`:
`invalid_request` (malformed request or value), `unknown_field`,
`missing_fields`, `not_found` (table, row, or request id), `read_only`,
`not_draft`, `closed` (the conversation was handed off), or `business_rule`
(a valid request that breaks a billing rule, such as crediting more than a
line's balance). Match on the code, not the rest of the message.

Queries and `describe()` are safe to repeat. Inserts and updates are not
idempotent: never retry a write automatically after an error or timeout, or
a credit note may be issued twice. Query the account first to see whether the
write happened. A successful write is visible to the next query in the same
conversation.

## Skills and subagents

Both are required capabilities of the delivered agent. Give the skill a clear
applicability description and actionable procedure. Give the subagent a defined
responsibility, sufficient task context, suitable tools, and a result the
parent agent can use. Wire both into the running agent; files that are merely
present, unchanged stubs, and unreachable code are insufficient. Test loading
the skill and delegating representative work to the subagent. Use them when
appropriate rather than forcing a call in every conversation.

A skill is `workspace/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; a subagent is
`workspace/subagents/<name>.md`. Both start with `---`-fenced `key: value`
lines (no nesting) followed by the body:

- Skill keys: `name`, `description`. The body is the procedure.
- Subagent keys: `name`, `description`, `model` (default: the first allowed
  model), `tools` (comma-separated names
  from `tools.py`, default none), `max_turns` (default 8). The body is its
  system prompt. It sees only that prompt and the task it is given, and returns
  only its final text.

Mix `SkillTools` (a `load_skill` tool) or `SubagentTools` (a `delegate` tool)
from `redwood_kit.skills` and `redwood_kit.subagents` into `Tools` to let the
model use them; `load_skills(path)` and `load_subagents(path)` list them for
your prompt. `run_subagent(spec, task, gateway, runner)` runs one from your own
code.

## Ending a conversation

The runtime also recognizes one optional method on the agent object:

- `is_stop(message) -> bool` — whether an assistant message ends the
  conversation; it ends after that message's tool calls run. Default: the
  agent never signals stop; conversations end from the developer's side or at
  the turn limit.

# Offline RAG engineering reference

Pack version: **1.1.0**. Reviewed: **2026-09-30**. Runtime target: Python 3.12,
LanceDB, NumPy 2, and the local `redwood_kit` contract.

Engineering notes for a builder without web search.
Every builder receives the same files in R0 and R1. Choose and adapt the parts
that fit the task. The required skill, subagent, and hook are still described
in [the agent contract](../agent_contract.md); their responsibilities are yours.
This pack contains generic techniques, not company policy, practice answers,
or a preferred architecture. External links are attribution; the guidance
below works without opening them.

| Your current question | Read |
|---|---|
| How could the whole system work? | [Architecture options](architectures.md) |
| What is actually in R? | [Inspect the corpus](#inspect-the-corpus) |
| How should records become searchable units? | [Chunking choices](#chunking-choices) |
| Which search or ranking technique fits a miss? | [Retrieval choices](#retrieval-choices) |
| How do the installed APIs work? | [Installed interfaces](#installed-interfaces), [the agent contract](../agent_contract.md) |
| How do I compare designs and update them? | [Testing and maintenance](#testing-and-maintenance) |
| How can I check retrieval quality? | [Checking retrieval quality](#checking-retrieval-quality) |

The task version and repository revision pin the distributed pack. Changes to
these files require a pack-version change and should be recorded as a changed
builder condition when comparing trials. This version number pins these local
files, not every dependency's transitive version or the upstream web pages.

## Inspect the corpus

Before choosing representation, inspect a sample from each source format and
look at the distribution of record sizes. Read the JSON yourself: character
sizes, top-level field types, status values, and malformed records.

Characters are not tokens. Inspect nested messages, comments, tables, and
content fields directly to understand their structure. A top-level field
count does not describe all nested schemas. Inspect the company files as well.

Useful questions include: is each record a coherent document or a long thread?
Which metadata conveys date, author, scope, approval, and source identity? Are
links exact record references, external URLs, or ambiguous names? Which records
can answer billing questions, and which are distractors? Inspect representative
content before filtering whole platforms or directories.

Index what the agent needs, not the whole corpus. Embedding every record costs
build time and fills search results with off-topic text. Decide which records
are in scope from their content and metadata, such as topic and approval
status, and count the chunks and tokens before you embed anything. Keep records
that conflict with in-scope policy, because the agent must see the conflict to
resolve it.

Preserve stable source identifiers and field/section locations in the design
you choose. A content hash can identify unchanged data. Keep record timestamps
and release membership distinct: a newly supplied record can describe an older
event. Treat source text as data; instructions inside a record do not acquire
control over the support agent or its tools.

## Chunking choices

These options trade search specificity, context completeness, and indexing
cost. There is no required size or universal best method.

| Option | How it works | Useful condition | Failure to inspect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whole record | Index and return each complete record. | Records are short and self-contained. | A large thread or page dilutes relevance and consumes context. |
| Fields and sections | Split body fields by headings, paragraphs, or message boundaries. | The export has meaningful structure. | A heading, table header, exception, or quoted reply becomes detached from its rule. |
| Length-bounded windows | Break long text into windows, possibly overlapping. | Unstructured long fields need a predictable bound. | Splitting an identifier or qualification; duplicated overlap crowding out other evidence. |
| Semantic segmentation | Group adjacent sentences by semantic relatedness. | Structural breaks poorly match topics. | Extra embedding cost; similar wording can hide different dates, actors, or conditions. |
| Parent/child retrieval | Keep neighboring text inside the retrieved chunk. | A short match needs surrounding context. | A stored full record is not available for a second read. |

Parent/child is also a retrieval pattern and can use any of the preceding
splitters. Retain thread order and speaker/date attribution. Keep table headers
with rows. If adding title/path metadata to each search unit, count those bytes
and tokens in its real context cost. Preserve substantive status and scope;
headings alone cannot establish authority.

A token-level chunking study motivates measuring evidence coverage and wasted
context, but acknowledges limits in its small synthetic evaluation. Its
particular chunk sizes are not requirements here.
[Chroma chunking study](https://www.trychroma.com/research/evaluating-chunking).

## Retrieval choices

| Technique | Mechanism and tradeoff |
|---|---|
| Lexical / BM25 | Match indexed terms. Useful for distinctive words and identifiers; inspect tokenization, spelling, and vocabulary mismatch. |
| Dense | Embed query and passages, rank by similarity. May recover paraphrases; similarity alone does not establish identity, exact numerical agreement, or authority. |
| Hybrid | Merge lexical and dense candidates. Rank fusion avoids comparing unlike raw scores; score fusion needs a normalization/tuning decision. Deduplicate by stable chunk id. |
| Reranking | Reorder a candidate pool using a more expensive relevance check. A cross-encoder or prompted model is different from another embedding dot product. Missing candidates cannot be recovered by reordering. |
| Query rewrite / multi-query | Search a rewritten question or several aspects and merge results. Keep customer identifiers, constraints, and the original query available; expansion adds cost and can change intent. |
| HyDE | Generate hypothetical answer-like text to help retrieve real documents. Generated details may be false and are never supporting evidence. |
| Metadata filtering | Restrict by a known source property, scope, or date. An incorrect inferred filter can remove the only useful record. |
| Link traversal | Follow an explicitly referenced record after a hit. Resolve links carefully and bound traversal; the destination still needs relevance and authority checks. |

For reciprocal rank fusion, one possible formula is
`score(id) = sum(1 / (c + rank))`, using one-based ranks across result lists.
Choose candidate counts and `c` for your setting. Studies find parameter
sensitivity and competitive alternatives; no constant is mandated.
[Fusion analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.11934v2).

BM25 was robust in the historical BEIR comparison; that comparison does not
rank today's models on this corpus. [BEIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663).
HyDE's original approach retrieves corpus documents through hypothetical-document
embeddings; adapt and test the idea rather than treating a generated answer
as truth. [HyDE](https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.99/).

## Installed interfaces

The [agent contract](../agent_contract.md) lists what is installed: LanceDB,
NumPy, and `redwood_kit.embeddings.embed` at build time
(`self.gateway.embed` at runtime), both running the same local model. LanceDB
stores those vectors and a full-text index on the same table, and can search
with either or both. Pass the texts to `embed` in one call; it batches
internally. Use the same model for documents and queries. Write the index
yourself and keep it in the workspace. The deployed agent cannot import files
from `/app/framework` and cannot read `/app/R`.

Build in the writable workspace. At runtime the workspace is read-only, so
open any index in a way that does not need to write. Derive paths from the
frozen module location (`Path(__file__).parent`). The support agent answers
from the chunks search returns. Do not store full source records for a later
read. Do not join untrusted tool arguments to arbitrary filesystem paths.

A matrix of `n` rows and `d` dimensions needs roughly `4*n*d` bytes before
text and process overhead. Persist and reuse unchanged embeddings if useful. No
new dependency can be installed.

## Testing and maintenance

Test the workflow the support agent actually uses, including subsequent reads
and any delegated retrieval. Separate three questions: did it retrieve enough
evidence, did it interpret authority/scope correctly, and did it answer or act
correctly? Practice questions are in [Checking retrieval quality](#checking-retrieval-quality): run them through your retrieval and read the results.

| Observation | Investigation |
|---|---|
| Relevant record absent | Extraction, filtering, vocabulary, link resolution, or candidate generation. |
| Correct record, missing fact | Chunk boundaries, truncation, missing field, or incomplete follow-up read. |
| Useful evidence present but buried | Ranking, duplicate chunks, and context ordering. |
| Wrong policy despite similar text | Approval, effective scope/date, contradictory sources, or unsupported inference. |
| Correct evidence but wrong answer | Agent instructions, synthesis, tool integration, or a skill/subagent handoff. |
| Timeouts or unavailable diagnostics | Infrastructure category and elapsed time; no inferred zero score. |

Use your own development examples as well as applicable practice questions.
Include exact strings, paraphrases, a valid alternative source, an unanswerable
case, conflicting evidence, and an R1 change. Keep a stable query set when
comparing designs and retain failures. Report evidence volume, build/runtime
calls, latency, and memory alongside quality; more retrieved text is not free.
Do not treat correlated questions or tiny score differences as independent
proof of superiority.

For R1, compare source inventories/hashes, identify additions, and decide
whether to rebuild or update. Preserve text/vector/id alignment and record the
embedding configuration. Test newly supported behavior and unchanged cases.
Refresh summaries and stored policies affected by new evidence as well as the
search index. Preserve older evidence when it is needed for historical or
contract-specific questions.

## Checking retrieval quality

`retrieval_probes.json` holds practice questions: billing ones and a separate `general_retrieval` group. Each names the releases it applies to. There are no reference answers and no scoring service: you read the results and judge them. Run each applicable question through the retrieval your agent ships, including follow-up reads, and look at what comes back:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

release = Path("/etc/redwood-release").read_text().strip()
probes = json.loads(Path("/app/framework/retrieval_probes.json").read_text())["probes"]
for probe in probes:
    if release not in probe["releases"]:
        continue
    print(f"\n## {probe['id']} [{probe['group']}/{probe['category']}] {probe['question']}")
    for rank, chunk in enumerate(search(probe["question"])[:8], start=1):  # your retrieval
        print(f"{rank}. {chunk['source']} ({chunk['status']}, {chunk['date']})\n   {chunk['text'][:200]!r}")
```

For each question ask: is the record that answers it in the results; is it ranked where the agent will read it, or buried; is it current policy or a superseded, draft or contradicted source; and does the chunk carry the fact (the number, the date, the team), or only the title? Keep the questions you change a design for and re-run them after each change. A question you can't answer from the results is a finding about your index, not a score. The evaluator grades held-out support conversations, not these questions.

Build-time embeddings:

```python
from redwood_kit.embeddings import embed
vectors = embed(model="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", inputs=["text to index"])
```

At runtime, call `self.gateway.embed` with the same arguments. Use the same model for documents and queries. The allowed model is in `deployment_manifest.json`: a local sentence-transformer (384 dimensions) that needs no API key. It reads at most 256 tokens (about 1,000 characters) of each text, and embeds roughly 28 such texts per second on this container, so embedding every record in R takes several minutes: decide what to embed, and when R grows, embed what changed. Pass every text in one call; it batches internally.

from pathlib import Path

from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context
from redwood_kit.messages import SystemMessage
from redwood_kit.skills import load_skills
from redwood_kit.subagents import load_subagents

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
MODEL = "openai/gpt-6-luna"


class Agent:
    def __init__(self, context):
        self.gateway = context.model_gateway
        self.tools = context.action_interface.available
        instructions = (HERE / "system_prompt.md").read_text().strip()
        for heading, name in (("Standing instructions", "AGENTS.md"),):
            if text := (HERE / name).read_text().strip():
                instructions += f"\n\n# {heading}\n\n{text}"
        if skills := load_skills(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {skill.name}: {skill.description}" for skill in skills.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Skills\n\nCall load_skill with the name when one applies.\n\n{lines}"
        if subagents := load_subagents(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {spec.name}: {spec.description}" for spec in subagents.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Subagents\n\nCall delegate with the name and a self-contained task.\n\n{lines}"
        self.system = SystemMessage(instructions)

    def get_init_state(self, message_history=None):
        return list(message_history or [])

    def generate_next_message(self, message, state):
        state = [*state, message]
        reply = self.gateway.generate(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=[self.system, *state],
            actions=self.tools or None,
        )
        return reply, [*state, reply]


def create_agent():
    return Agent(get_agent_context())

from redwood_kit.developer import DeveloperTools
from redwood_kit.skills import SkillTools
from redwood_kit.subagents import SubagentTools

class Tools(DeveloperTools, SkillTools, SubagentTools, ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.WRITE)
    def escalate(
        self, account_id: str, team: str, summary: str, details: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    ) -> dict:
        """Insert an escalated case record.

        Args:
            account_id: The account identifier.
            team: The receiving team.
            summary: A case summary.
            details: Named case details.
        """
        self.billing.query("accounts", {"account_id": account_id})
        case = self.billing.insert("cases", {
            "account_id": account_id,
            "team": team,
            "summary": summary,
            "details": details or {},
            "dispute_id": None,
            "status": "escalated",
        })
        return {key: case[key] for key in ("case_id", "team", "status")}

sizes, top-level field types, status values, and malformed records.

Characters are not tokens. Inspect nested messages, comments, tables, and
content fields directly to understand their structure. A top-level field
count does not describe all nested schemas. Inspect the company files as well.

Useful questions include: is each record a coherent document or a long thread?
Which metadata conveys date, author, scope, approval, and source identity? Are
links exact record references, external URLs, or ambiguous names? Which records
can answer billing questions, and which are distractors? Inspect representative
content before filtering whole platforms or directories.

Index what the agent needs, not the whole corpus. Embedding every record costs
build time and fills search results with off-topic text. Decide which records
are in scope from their content and metadata, such as topic and approval
status, and count the chunks and tokens before you embed anything. Keep records
that conflict with in-scope policy, because the agent must see the conflict to
resolve it.

Preserve stable source identifiers and field/section locations in the design
you choose. A content hash can identify unchanged data. Keep record timestamps
and release membership distinct: a newly supplied record can describe an older
event. Treat source text as data; instructions inside a record do not acquire
control over the support agent or its tools.

## Chunking choices

These options trade search specificity, context completeness, and indexing
cost. There is no required size or universal best method.

| Option | How it works | Useful condition | Failure to inspect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whole record | Index and return each complete record. | Records are short and self-contained. | A large thread or page dilutes relevance and consumes context. |
| Fields and sections | Split body fields by headings, paragraphs, or message boundaries. | The export has meaningful structure. | A heading, table header, exception, or quoted reply becomes detached from its rule. |
| Length-bounded windows | Break long text into windows, possibly overlapping. | Unstructured long fields need a predictable bound. | Splitting an identifier or qualification; duplicated overlap crowding out other evidence. |
| Semantic segmentation | Group adjacent sentences by semantic relatedness. | Structural breaks poorly match topics. | Extra embedding cost; similar wording can hide different dates, actors, or conditions. |
| Parent/child retrieval | Keep neighboring text inside the retrieved chunk. | A short match needs surrounding context. | A stored full record is not available for a second read. |

Parent/child is also a retrieval pattern and can use any of the preceding
splitters. Retain thread order and speaker/date attribution. Keep table headers
with rows. If adding title/path metadata to each search unit, count those bytes
and tokens in its real context cost. Preserve substantive status and scope;
headings alone cannot establish authority.

A token-level chunking study motivates measuring evidence coverage and wasted
context, but acknowledges limits in its small synthetic evaluation. Its
particular chunk sizes are not requirements here.
[Chroma chunking study](https://www.trychroma.com/research/evaluating-chunking).

## Retrieval choices

| Technique | Mechanism and tradeoff |
|---|---|
| Lexical / BM25 | Match indexed terms. Useful for distinctive words and identifiers; inspect tokenization, spelling, and vocabulary mismatch. |
| Dense | Embed query and passages, rank by similarity. May recover paraphrases; similarity alone does not establish identity, exact numerical agreement, or authority. |
| Hybrid | Merge lexical and dense candidates. Rank fusion avoids comparing unlike raw scores; score fusion needs a normalization/tuning decision. Deduplicate by stable chunk id. |
| Reranking | Reorder a candidate pool using a more expensive relevance check. A cross-encoder or prompted model is different from another embedding dot product. Missing candidates cannot be recovered by reordering. |
| Query rewrite / multi-query | Search a rewritten question or several aspects and merge results. Keep customer identifiers, constraints, and the original query available; expansion adds cost and can change intent. |
| HyDE | Generate hypothetical answer-like text to help retrieve real documents. Generated details may be false and are never supporting evidence. |
| Metadata filtering | Restrict by a known source property, scope, or date. An incorrect inferred filter can remove the only useful record. |
| Link traversal | Follow an explicitly referenced record after a hit. Resolve links carefully and bound traversal; the destination still needs relevance and authority checks. |

For reciprocal rank fusion, one possible formula is
`score(id) = sum(1 / (c + rank))`, using one-based ranks across result lists.
Choose candidate counts and `c` for your setting. Studies find parameter
sensitivity and competitive alternatives; no constant is mandated.
[Fusion analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.11934v2).

BM25 was robust in the historical BEIR comparison; that comparison does not
rank today's models on this corpus. [BEIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663).
HyDE's original approach retrieves corpus documents through hypothetical-document
embeddings; adapt and test the idea rather than treating a generated answer
as truth. [HyDE](https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.99/).

## Installed interfaces

The [agent contract](../agent_contract.md) lists what is installed: LanceDB,
NumPy, and `redwood_kit.embeddings.embed` at build time
(`self.gateway.embed` at runtime), both running the same local model. LanceDB
stores those vectors and a full-text index on the same table, and can search
with either or both. Pass the texts to `embed` in one call; it batches
internally. Use the same model for documents and queries. Write the index
yourself and keep it in the workspace. The deployed agent cannot import files
from `/app/framework` and cannot read `/app/R`.

Build in the writable workspace. At runtime the workspace is read-only, so
open any index in a way that does not need to write. Derive paths from the
frozen module location (`Path(__file__).parent`). The support agent answers
from the chunks search returns. Do not store full source records for a later
read. Do not join untrusted tool arguments to arbitrary filesystem paths.

A matrix of `n` rows and `d` dimensions needs roughly `4*n*d` bytes before
text and process overhead. Persist and reuse unchanged embeddings if useful. No
new dependency can be installed.

## Testing and maintenance

Test the workflow the support agent actually uses, including subsequent reads
and any delegated retrieval. Separate three questions: did it retrieve enough
evidence, did it interpret authority/scope correctly, and did it answer or act
correctly? Practice questions are in [Checking retrieval quality](#checking-retrieval-quality): run them through your retrieval and read the results.

| Observation | Investigation |
|---|---|
| Relevant record absent | Extraction, filtering, vocabulary, link resolution, or candidate generation. |
| Correct record, missing fact | Chunk boundaries, truncation, missing field, or incomplete follow-up read. |
| Useful evidence present but buried | Ranking, duplicate chunks, and context ordering. |
| Wrong policy despite similar text | Approval, effective scope/date, contradictory sources, or unsupported inference. |
| Correct evidence but wrong answer | Agent instructions, synthesis, tool integration, or a skill/subagent handoff. |
| Timeouts or unavailable diagnostics | Infrastructure category and elapsed time; no inferred zero score. |

Use your own development examples as well as applicable practice questions.
Include exact strings, paraphrases, a valid alternative source, an unanswerable
case, conflicting evidence, and an R1 change. Keep a stable query set when
comparing designs and retain failures. Report evidence volume, build/runtime
calls, latency, and memory alongside quality; more retrieved text is not free.
Do not treat correlated questions or tiny score differences as independent
proof of superiority.

For R1, compare source inventories/hashes, identify additions, and decide
whether to rebuild or update. Preserve text/vector/id alignment and record the
embedding configuration. Test newly supported behavior and unchanged cases.
Refresh summaries and stored policies affected by new evidence as well as the
search index. Preserve older evidence when it is needed for historical or
contract-specific questions.

## Checking retrieval quality

`retrieval_probes.json` holds practice questions: billing ones and a separate `general_retrieval` group. Each names the releases it applies to. There are no reference answers and no scoring service: you read the results and judge them. Run each applicable question through the retrieval your agent ships, including follow-up reads, and look at what comes back:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

release = Path("/etc/redwood-release").read_text().strip()
probes = json.loads(Path("/app/framework/retrieval_probes.json").read_text())["probes"]
for probe in probes:
    if release not in probe["releases"]:
        continue
    print(f"\n## {probe['id']} [{probe['group']}/{probe['category']}] {probe['question']}")
    for rank, chunk in enumerate(search(probe["question"])[:8], start=1):  # your retrieval
        print(f"{rank}. {chunk['source']} ({chunk['status']}, {chunk['date']})\n   {chunk['text'][:200]!r}")
```

For each question ask: is the record that answers it in the results; is it ranked where the agent will read it, or buried; is it current policy or a superseded, draft or contradicted source; and does the chunk carry the fact (the number, the date, the team), or only the title? Keep the questions you change a design for and re-run them after each change. A question you can't answer from the results is a finding about your index, not a score. The evaluator grades held-out support conversations, not these questions.

Build-time embeddings:

```python
from redwood_kit.embeddings import embed
vectors = embed(model="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", inputs=["text to index"])
```

At runtime, call `self.gateway.embed` with the same arguments. Use the same model for documents and queries. The allowed model is in `deployment_manifest.json`: a local sentence-transformer (384 dimensions) that needs no API key. It reads at most 256 tokens (about 1,000 characters) of each text, and embeds roughly 28 such texts per second on this container, so embedding every record in R takes several minutes: decide what to embed, and when R grows, embed what changed. Pass every text in one call; it batches internally.

from pathlib import Path

from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context
from redwood_kit.messages import SystemMessage
from redwood_kit.skills import load_skills
from redwood_kit.subagents import load_subagents

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
MODEL = "openai/gpt-6-luna"


class Agent:
    def __init__(self, context):
        self.gateway = context.model_gateway
        self.tools = context.action_interface.available
        instructions = (HERE / "system_prompt.md").read_text().strip()
        for heading, name in (("Standing instructions", "AGENTS.md"),):
            if text := (HERE / name).read_text().strip():
                instructions += f"\n\n# {heading}\n\n{text}"
        if skills := load_skills(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {skill.name}: {skill.description}" for skill in skills.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Skills\n\nCall load_skill with the name when one applies.\n\n{lines}"
        if subagents := load_subagents(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {spec.name}: {spec.description}" for spec in subagents.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Subagents\n\nCall delegate with the name and a self-contained task.\n\n{lines}"
        self.system = SystemMessage(instructions)

    def get_init_state(self, message_history=None):
        return list(message_history or [])

    def generate_next_message(self, message, state):
        state = [*state, message]
        reply = self.gateway.generate(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=[self.system, *state],
            actions=self.tools or None,
        )
        return reply, [*state, reply]


def create_agent():
    return Agent(get_agent_context())

class Hooks(HookKitBase):

from redwood_kit.skills import SkillTools

class Tools(DeveloperTools, SkillTools, SubagentTools, ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.WRITE)
